content:
# Semantic-Anchor Checkpoints in the Ghost-AOS Git-Bus Treaty

## 1. The problem, stated exactly

A seat's context is a token sequence. Any byte change before the head — redaction, compaction, injected system note, rebase onto a moved topic ref — naively invalidates the entire KV prefix and forces a full re-prefill. For a stateless seat that dies and respawns, the situation is worse: the naive respawn replays the whole context through prefill every time, even when nothing changed. The fix is structural, not statistical: **make the context an append-only chain of immutable, content-addressed segments, and place anchors at the only points where edits are legally allowed to cut.** Then "edit" always means "fork the chain at an anchor," and the re-prefill set is provably the suffix from that anchor forward — nothing more.

The git-bus gives us the persistence substrate for free: blobs are immutable and content-addressed, trees are Merkle proofs over segment order, commits are atomic transitions, refs are the head pointers a respawned seat needs. The treaty's job is to forbid the operations that would break cache resumability.

---

## 2. Core invariant

> **Every committed context state is a tree of immutable segment blobs. Every legal edit begins at a declared anchor. Therefore the set of tokens requiring prefill after any transition or respawn is exactly `[anchor_token_offset, head_token_offset)`, and every token before it is reusable by anyone holding the same chain hashes, model revision, and tokenizer.**

Everything below is machinery to make that sentence true and checkable.

---

## 3. Data model on the bus

### 3.1 Objects

```
refs/bus/<topic>/<seat>          # seat-private head, fast-forward only
refs/topics/<topic>              # merged topic head, fast-forward only
refs/leases/<seat>               # epoch counter, CAS-updated

<commit>  per context transition
  parent   = previous state commit
  tree     = ContextTree
  trailers:
    Op:                 append | splice | compact | promote-draft
    FirstChangedAnchor: <ordinal>          # re-prefill starts here
    ReprefillTokens:    <int>              # honest cost, hook-verified
    Epoch:              <int>
    Lease:              <lease-id>

<tree> ContextTree
  000001 -> blob : sys_preamble
  000002 -> blob : msg_user_1
  000003 -> blob : msg_asst_1
  000004 -> blob : tool_result_1
  ...

<blob> Segment            # canonical CBOR, one message/tool-result/summary
<blob> Manifest           # the anchor checkpoint itself (below)
<blob> Draft              # lives OUTSIDE the context tree, under drafts/
```

### 3.2 The Manifest (this is the checkpoint)

```cbor
{
  v: 2,
  model:     { id: "...", rev: "sha256:..." },
  tokenizer: { hash: "sha256:...", vocab_rev: 17 },
  rope:      { scaling: null, theta: 10000 },
  positions: "contiguous",
  cache_salt: "sha256:<deployment_id || model_rev>",   # NOT per-seat
  anchors: [
    { ord: 0,  seg: "000001", tok_end: 312,    byte_end: 1204,   kind: "system" },
    { ord: 1,  seg: "000002", tok_end: 1180,   byte_end: 4410,   kind: "turn" },
    ...
    { ord: 31, seg: "000041", tok_end: 49664,  byte_end: 198113, kind: "turn" }
  ],
  subanchors: [
    { ord: 31, tok_offsets: [47104, 47616, 48128, 48640, 49152] }  # 512-tok grid
  ]
}
```

The manifest is what lets a respawned seat skip tokenization entirely: byte↔token offsets are recorded at write time, verified lazily.

### 3.3 Chain keys (the serving-layer cache key)

```
K_0 = H("ghost-aos/v2" || model.rev)
K_i = H(K_{i-1} || h(seg_i))
```

Cumulative hash chain, domain-separated by model revision. Two seats (or two lives of one seat) with identical prefixes compute identical `K_i` — this is what makes cross-seat and cross-respawn prefix reuse possible. Computing the chain is O(n) hashing over 32-byte digests: microseconds, no tokenization, no model contact.

---

## 4. Anchor taxonomy and placement policy

| Kind | Placed at | Granularity | Stored as |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hard anchor** | End of system preamble; end of every committed turn; end of every tool result; compaction seams | Wherever the turn ends | Tree ordinal + manifest row |
| **Soft anchor** | Inside long segments (>1024 tok): paragraph boundaries snapped to the KV block grid | Every ~512 tokens | Offsets inside one manifest row |

Two rules that matter:

1. **Block alignment.** Paged KV caches reuse per-block (typically 16 tokens). Snap soft anchors to block boundaries. A hard anchor falling mid-block costs at most one partial-block recompute (≤15 tokens) — noise.
2. **Contiguous positions.** Absolute position IDs run 0..T with no re-indexing, so an anchor's KV is valid at its recorded offsets forever. If anyone introduces relative/re-based positions, the manifest gains a `pos_base` per anchor or reuse claims are void. Default design forbids re-indexing.

**Why semantic, not fixed-interval:** real edits target things — redact the PII in turn 17, compact turns 3–14, inject a policy note after the preamble. Turn-aligned hard anchors make those cuts land *exactly*, for zero wasted re-prefill. Fixed intervals would eat an average half-interval of waste per edit and still miss. Soft anchors exist only so a splice into a long document lands within 512 tokens of intent instead of within 40k.

---

## 5. Edit operations and the cost rule

| Op | Effect on chain | FirstChangedAnchor | ReprefillTokens |
|---|---|---|---|
| `append` | New segments after head | none (head) | 0 (new tokens only) |
| `splice` (insert/redact/replace) | Fork at anchor *a*: prefix tree identical, suffix rebuilt | *a* | head_tok − anchor_tok(*a*) |
| `compact` | Segments [i..j] replaced by summary blob | *i* | head_tok − anchor_tok(*i*) |
| `promote-draft` | Draft blob becomes canonical segment | none | 0 |

**The cost rule (enforced, not aspirational):** an editor must cut at the *deepest* anchor ≤ its intended edit point. The commit hook recomputes `ReprefillTokens` from the manifest and rejects the push if the claimed anchor is shallower than the deepest legal one. Editors pay honestly; schedulers can price transitions; nobody discovers a 200k-token re-prefill at respawn time.

**Compaction is never free.** It breaks the chain at seam *i* and everything after re-prefills. The treaty does not hide this — it records it. Guidance: compact at the oldest viable anchor, batch rarely. There is no prefix-preserving compaction trick; a different byte sequence is a different cache. Say so in the commit and move on.

---

## 6. Stateless seat: death and respawn, step by step

**Death.** Seat S, epoch 7, dies mid-decode. Head = commit C₄₁ (tree T₄₁, manifest M₄₁, head at token 49,664). Last draft blob covers generated tokens 49,665–49,920 (committed every 128 generated tokens, async, best-effort). Final ~80 tokens are lost. Nothing else in-process matters.

**Respawn (epoch 8):**

1. **Lease.** CAS `refs/leases/<seat>`: epoch 7 → 8. Stale-epoch pushes rejected thereafter. Single writer guaranteed.
2. **Resolve head.** Fetch `refs/bus/<topic>/<seat>` → C₄₁ → T₄₁ + M₄₁. Integrity is inherent: git object hashes verify the tree against the blobs on arrival.
3. **Compatibility gate.** Compare `M.model.rev` and `M.tokenizer.hash` against the serving target. Match → proceed. Mismatch → **all reuse claims void**, full re-prefill, emit a treaty warning event, write a fresh manifest under the new rev.
4. **Compute chain keys** `K_1..K_n` from the tree's segment hashes. Microseconds.
5. **Gateway resume call:** `resume(chain=[K_1..K_n], head_tok=49664)`. Gateway walks its radix/prefix cache on the cumulative keys and reports `hit_upto` in blocks.
   - **Hot case** (cache retained the seat's blocks, typical for fast respawn): `hit_upto` = full head. Prefill = **0 tokens**. Attach and decode.
   - **Warm case** (partial eviction): prefill from `hit_upto×block_size` to 49,664.
   - **Cold case** (evicted, or new backend): one full prefill of 49,664 tokens. Correctness unaffected; this is the latency floor the whole design drives toward rarely paying.
6. **Draft tail (optional, flag-gated).** `trust_drafts: false` for reasoning seats — regenerate the lost ~80 tokens fresh; drafts are advisory, never canonical. `true` for transcription-style seats — replay the draft tail as forced prompt tokens and continue from 49,921. Either way the draft blob is outside the tree until a live seat promotes it via `promote-draft`.
7. **Continue.** Commit cadence: every completed assistant turn = canonical commit; every 128 generated tokens = draft blob push.

**Multi-writer note:** seat heads are seat-private, so there is no write contention on them. Topic heads advance by fast-forward-only merge of seat commits. A non-fast-forward (topic moved underneath you) forces a rebase, which is a splice at the merge seam — cost bounded to post-seam tokens by the same anchor rule.

---

## 7. The ledger: what persists vs. what recomputes

| Item | Persisted? | Where | Respawn cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Context segments (bytes) | **Yes** | git blobs, immutable | 0 |
| State trees + transition commits | **Yes** | git trees/commits | 0 |
| Anchor manifest (offsets, kinds, subanchors) | **Yes** | manifest blob | 0 |
| Model rev / tokenizer hash / rope / salt pins | **Yes** | manifest | 0 |
| Draft tails (best-effort, non-canonical) | Mostly | draft blobs | regenerate ≤128 tok, or replay if trusted |
| Chain keys K_i | No — derived | — | O(n) SHA-256, µs–ms |
| Tokenization | No — offsets pre-recorded | manifest | verify-only or skipped |
| KV tensors | **No** | serving-layer cache only | 0 on hit; O(tokens) prefill on miss |
| In-flight decode state (logits, sampler state) | No | — | n/a; fresh sample from last boundary |
| Tool scratch, embeddings, indexes, working views | No | — | rebuilt deterministically from blobs |

The asymmetry is the point: **everything semantic persists as hashes; everything heavy is either someone else's cache keyed by our hashes, or derivable in milliseconds.**

---

## 8. Serving-layer contract

- Accepts `resume(chain, head_tok)`; keys its radix/prefix cache on `K_i`.
- Reports `hit_upto` in blocks; prefills only `(hit_upto·B, head_tok]`.
- Treats `cache_salt` as global-per-deployment (`model_rev ‖ deployment_id`), **not per-seat** — so N seats sharing a system preamble share those blocks. Isolation comes from refs, not from salt.
- Never stores KV under a key without a complete manifest pin (model rev + tokenizer hash + rope). Missing pin ⇒ uncacheable, full prefill.

---

## 9. Treaty clauses (server-enforceable)

- **T1 Immutability.** Bus refs are fast-forward-only; force-push rejected. A blob referenced by any committed tree never changes bytes.
- **T2 Anchored edits.** Every splice/compact commit declares `FirstChangedAnchor`; the hook recomputes the deepest legal anchor from the manifest and rejects shallower cuts. `ReprefillTokens` is hook-computed, not author-claimed.
- **T3 Pin completeness.** Manifests lacking model rev + tokenizer hash are invalid; consumers must refuse cache reuse.
- **T4 Atomic transitions.** One commit per transition; intermediate trees never pushed.
- **T5 Lease exclusivity.** One writer per seat ref per epoch; epoch CAS on lease ref.
- **T6 Canonical bytes.** Deterministic CBOR (sorted keys, fixed widths, UTF-8 NFC, `\n`) — otherwise hashes aren't reproducible across seats and the whole scheme rots.
- **T7 Draft hygiene.** Drafts live outside the context tree; promotion requires a fresh commit from a live lease holder. A dead seat's half-thought never becomes canon.

---

## 10. Failure modes and counters

- **Serving-cache eviction between death and respawn** → cold full prefill. Correct, slow. Track `anchor_hit_ratio` per respawn; it's the design's vital sign.
- **Tokenizer/model upgrade mid-flight** → T3 gate forces full re-prefill exactly once, then a fresh manifest lineage. Never silently mix.
- **Coarse anchors** → subanchors at 512-token block-aligned grids inside long segments.
- **Non-canonical serialization** → T6 + hash verification on fetch; a bad encoder fails loudly at push time, not at respawn.
- **Rebase storms on hot topics** → each rebase is a splice; cost is bounded and priced by T2. If a topic rebases more often than seats finish turns, that's a treaty-violating workflow, not a cache problem.

---

## 11. Grounding numbers

200k-token context, 16-token blocks:

- **Hot respawn** (died, restarted in seconds): 0 prefill tokens. Resume is lease-CAS + ref fetch + hash chain + cache attach: tens of milliseconds of CPU, zero GPU prefill.
- **Deep redaction** of one tool result at anchor 31 (tok 49,664 of 200,000): re-prefill = 150,336 tokens… which is why T2 forces the *deepest* anchor — the same redaction targeting a tool result at anchor 29 (tok 41,000) is illegal if the cut could land at 30. When the edit genuinely targets late content, cost is honest and unavoidable; when it doesn't, it's zero.
- **Frequent small edits near the head**: re-prefill in the hundreds of tokens, versus 200k naive — three orders of magnitude.
- **Compaction of turns 3–14** ending at anchor 12 (tok 18,240): re-prefill = 181,760 tokens, paid once, recorded in the commit, visible to every scheduler on the bus.

The design's entire payoff reduces to one measurable claim: **after any transition or respawn, prefill work equals `head − FirstChangedAnchor`, and nothing else — verifiable from the commit trailer, reproducible from the manifest, and enforced by the hook.**
reasoning:
The user is asking about a hard systems design problem: "semantic-anchor checkpoints so an agent's context edit re-prefills only the new suffix, in the Ghost-AOS git-bus treaty. Design it for a stateless seat that dies and respawns: what persists vs recomputes."

This is a fictional/constructed system — "Ghost-AOS git-bus treaty" appears to be a made-up framework, likely from the user's own project or a roleplay context ("Ghost's thousand-ask mining engine"). The system prompt says I'm "ox-alpha" and I'm "Ghost's thousand-ask mining engine." So this is a creative-technical exercise: design a concrete mechanism for semantic-anchor checkpoints in a git-based message bus for agent orchestration, where an agent's seat is stateless (dies and respawns), and when a context edit happens, only the new suffix gets re-prefilled (i.e., KV-cache-friendly incremental prefill).

Let me think about what this actually means technically:

**Domain mapping:**
- LLM serving: prompt prefix caching / KV cache reuse. When you edit a conversation's context (e.g., insert a system note, compact old turns), naive implementations invalidate the whole cache and re-prefill everything. The goal: structure the context as a chain of segments with stable anchors so that edits only invalidate from the edit point onward — i.e., re-prefill only the suffix after the last unchanged anchor.
- Git-bus treaty: a coordination protocol where agents communicate via a git repository as a bus — commits are messages, refs are topics/seats, merges are state reconciliation. A "treaty" is the agreed invariants.
- Stateless seat: the agent process holds no durable memory; it dies and respawns, reconstructing its working state from the bus (git objects) plus whatever checkpoint artifacts persist.
- Semantic-anchor checkpoints: checkpoints placed at semantically meaningful boundaries (not arbitrary token counts) such that content before the anchor is immutable (content-addressed, hash-pinned) and thus its KV cache can be reused across respawn and across edits.

**Core design problem:** For a stateless seat to resume cheaply, it needs:
1. A persistent record of which prefixes are valid and their hashes (so the inference backend's prefix cache can be keyed).
2. Immutable-by-construction history: append-only log where each entry references the hash of the previous context state (like a Merkle chain). Edits create a fork: new branch from the deepest unchanged anchor.
3. Anchor selection policy: anchors at turn boundaries, tool-result boundaries, compaction boundaries — points where the byte-level content is frozen forever.
4. What persists vs recomputes:
   - Persists: the git objects themselves (context segments as blobs/trees), anchor manifest (hash → segment id, token offsets, model+tokenizer version, sampling params affecting cache validity), the seat's lease/epoch record, the pointer to the live head.
   - Recomputes: anything not pinned — e.g., the actual KV tensors if the serving layer evicted them (recompute on demand via prefill of the anchored prefix, which may hit the cluster-wide prefix cache), ephemeral scratch, in-flight partial generations.

**Key subtlety: what makes a prefix reusable?**
KV cache validity depends on: exact token sequence, tokenizer version, model weights version, RoPE position base / context extension params, attention implementation details (sliding window vs full), sampling doesn't matter for prefill but does for decode continuation. So the anchor manifest must pin: model id + revision, tokenizer hash, rope scaling config, and the exact byte range → token range mapping.

**Edit semantics:**
An "edit" to context = any operation that changes bytes before the current head: insertion of a system reminder, redaction, compaction (summarize turns 1..k into a summary block), truncation. Naive: full invalidation. With anchors: the edit must be expressed as a splice at an anchor boundary. If the edit point falls mid-segment, you have two options: (a) split the segment at the nearest prior anchor and accept re-prefill from there; (b) define sub-anchors within large segments (paragraph/sentence level) at write time so future splices land on one.

So the design: every segment is written once, hashed, never mutated. An edit produces a new tree: [prefix tree unchanged] + [replacement suffix]. The "re-prefill set" = tokens from the first changed byte onward. If the editor respects anchor boundaries, the first changed byte = an anchor start, and everything before is cache-hit.

**Git-bus encoding:**
- Refs: `refs/bus/<topic>/<seat>` for per-seat heads; `refs/anchors/<seat>` maybe. Or tags for anchors.
- Objects: 
  - `ctxseg` blobs: raw context chunks (messages serialized canonically).
  - Trees representing ordered concatenation: tree entries named by ordinal `000001`, pointing to blob + mode; the tree hash = context-state hash.
  - Commit per state transition with parent = previous state commit; commit message carries metadata: actor, op type (append/splice/compact), first-changed-offset, anchor id invalidated-from.
  - Manifest object (a special blob or annotated tag): maps anchor ordinals → {byte offset, token offset, seg hash, model rev, tokenizer hash}.
- Treaty invariants (the "treaty" part): 
  1. Immutability: committed segments are read-only; violation = treaty breach, refuse merge.
  2. Anchored splices: all edits must begin at an anchor boundary OR declare the fallback anchor explicitly (paying re-prefill cost honestly).
  3. Cache-key completeness: manifests must pin model/tokenizer/rope; mismatch ⇒ no reuse claim.
  4. Lease/epoch: a seat writes under a lease; on death, the lease expires and a successor reads the last committed head — no half-written states because commits are atomic.
  5. Deterministic serialization: canonical JSON/CBOR with sorted keys, fixed newline discipline, so byte hashes are reproducible across seats.

**Stateless seat lifecycle:**
1. Spawn: read `refs/bus/<topic>/<seat>` head → get commit → tree → manifest.
2. Reconstruct logical context: materialize segments (or just pass hashes to the serving layer if the serving layer has the blobs cached).
3. Prefill strategy: send the manifest to the router/inference gateway; gateway checks its prefix cache (keyed by tree-hash-prefix chains); hits serve KV directly (if it stores KV) or skip recompute (if it stores only token-block hashes à la vLLM automatic prefix caching / SGLang RadixAttention); misses trigger prefill of missing blocks only.
4. Decode continues from tail.
5. On death: nothing in-process matters. Everything needed is: head ref (persisted), manifest (persisted), segment blobs (persisted). Recompute: KV blocks evicted from serving cache; the tail partial generation (either discarded or committed as a draft blob before death — better: commit drafts frequently).

**What persists vs recomputes — the exact ledger:**

Persists (in git objects / refs):
- Every committed context segment (blob) — content-addressed, immutable.
- Ordered trees per state (Merkle over segments).
- Commits with transition metadata (op, first_changed_anchor, parent).
- Anchor manifest: anchor boundaries (segment ordinals), byte→token offsets, tokenizer hash, model rev, rope params, cache-salt.
- Seat identity + epoch counter (monotonic, in ref or in a lease file).
- Draft/partial outputs if the seat commits them before dying (checkpoint cadence).
- Compaction artifacts: summary segments replacing spans, with provenance pointers to replaced span hashes.

Recomputes (never persisted):
- KV tensors (owned by serving layer; may be cached there but that's the serving layer's business, keyed by our hashes).
- Tokenization results beyond stored offsets (though storing token offsets in manifest means even tokenization is mostly avoided; but re-tokenization is cheap and used to verify).
- In-flight decode state (last sampled token logits etc.) — restart decodes from last committed assistant boundary or last draft checkpoint.
- Ephemeral tool-call scratch, working memory derived views (indexes, embeddings) — rebuildable from blobs deterministically.

**Anchor placement policy (concrete):**
- Hard anchors: end of each committed message/turn; end of each tool result; end of system preamble; compaction seams.
- Soft/sub-anchors within long segments: every N tokens (e.g., 512) at paragraph boundaries, recorded in manifest as secondary offsets — these allow finer-grained splice landing without bloating git object count (sub-anchors are offsets inside one blob, not separate blobs).
- Rule: an editor must target the deepest anchor ≤ intended edit point. Cost accounting: re-prefill tokens = head_token_offset − anchor_token_offset. The treaty requires editors to record this cost in the commit metadata so schedulers can price it.

**Cache keying & the "only the new suffix" guarantee:**
- Define ContextStateId = tree hash. PrefixChain = list of segment hashes [h1..hk]. Serving-layer radix/prefix cache keyed by cumulative hash chains: key_i = H(h1||...||hi). Because segments are append-only and splices preserve the prefix chain up to the splice anchor, all keys up to anchor k match → blocks reused.
- New suffix = segments k+1..n plus the edited replacement. Only those get prefilled.
- Edge case: position ids. If we use standard contiguous positions, prefix reuse is trivially valid. If we ever do relative/re-indexed positions, manifest must store the position base per anchor. Keep it simple: contiguous 0..T positions, so anchor at token offset t has absolute positions baked in — reuse safe.

**Death/respawn walk-through (make it concrete):**
Seat S, epoch 7, dies mid-decode at token 48,112 of context length 50,000.
- Last committed state: commit C_41, tree T_41, manifest M_41 with anchors at token offsets [0(sys), 312, 1,204, ..., 49,664(last user turn)].
- Draft blob D (assistant partial, tokens 49,664→48,112... wait ordering—let me say context ends at 49,664; draft covers generated tokens 49,665..50,000-ish). Actually let me keep numbers clean: context head at token 49,664. Draft = 336 generated tokens, committed every 128 tokens as draft blobs appended to a `drafts/` area with parent links.
- Respawn: epoch 8. Read head → C_41. Read latest draft blob (tokens 49,665–49,920 committed; final 80 tokens lost). Gateway prefix-cache lookup on chain keys: full hit through anchor at 49,664 (assuming serving cache retained; if evicted, one prefill pass over 49,664 tokens — still correct, just slower; the design's job is to make the *hit* possible and verifiable).
- Resume decode from token 49,921 regenerating the last ~80 tokens. Regeneration divergence is fine: sampling is stochastic; treaty says drafts are advisory, committed assistant turns are canonical.

Hmm — should drafts be canonical? Better: two-tier. Drafts = resumable hints (non-canonical, marked `draft:true`, excluded from context tree). Committed turns = canonical, enter the tree. This avoids the problem of a dead seat's half-thought becoming gospel.

**Compaction interplay:**
Compaction replaces segments [i..j] with summary segment s. This breaks the chain at anchor i — everything from i onward is a re-prefill. Treaty guidance: compact at the oldest possible anchor, batch infrequently, and record `first_changed_anchor` so operators see the true cost. Alternative advanced move: "prefix-preserving compaction" — keep original segments physically in the tree but mark a view; views break cache anyway, so no free lunch; be honest: compaction costs a re-prefill from seam.

Actually, there's a subtle trick worth mentioning: if the serving layer supports it, you can keep TWO chains hot — the old full chain (for reference queries) and the new compacted chain — but that doubles cache pressure. Default: pay the re-prefill.

**Concurrency / multi-writer:**
Git-bus implies multiple seats may append to shared topic refs. Treaty: per-seat heads are seat-private (no contention); topic heads advance via fast-forward-only merges of seat commits; conflicts = non-fast-forward ⇒ reject, force rebase onto new topic head, which itself is a splice ⇒ re-prefill from the merge seam. Anchors make the rebase cost bounded to post-seam tokens.

**Verification / trust:**
Because everything is hash-chained, a respawned seat can verify integrity: recompute tree hash from blobs, compare to commit. Tokenizer drift detection: manifest stores tokenizer hash; if current tokenizer differs, all reuse claims void — full re-prefill, and emit a treaty warning event.

**Failure modes to nail down:**
- Serving cache eviction between death and respawn: correctness unaffected; latency = full prefill. Design metric: "anchor hit ratio" tracked per respawn.
- Non-deterministic serialization breaking hashes: mandate canonical encoding (CBOR deterministic profile or JSON with sorted keys, UTF-8 NFC, \n endings).
- Anchor granularity too coarse: big segments mean splices land far from intent. Mitigate with sub-anchors (offsets, not objects).
- Manifest bloat: manifests are small (one row per anchor); fine.
- Model upgrade mid-flight: model rev pinned per manifest; a seat respawning onto a new model rev must full-reprefill; treaty says bump a `cache_epoch` and invalidate globally.

```
    ...

  subanchors: [{anchor_ord:k, tok_offsets:[...]}],

```

Commit metadata (trailers):
```
Op: append|splice|compact|draft
FirstChangedAnchor: 12      // re-prefill starts here
ReprefillTokens: 8421       // honest cost

```

Serving-layer contract:
- `prefill(chain=[h1..hk], from_tok=t)` → returns handle; internally checks radix cache on cumulative keys; reuses blocks for keys matching up to largest i with key match and tok offset ≥ t alignment (block-size aligned, e.g., 16-token blocks; note: block alignment means effective reuse granularity is block-aligned anchors — mention that anchors should be recorded at block-aligned token offsets where possible, or accept partial-block recompute of ≤15 tokens).

Ah, important detail: paged KV caches work in blocks (e.g., 16 tokens). Prefix cache hits are per-block. So an anchor at token 49,664: 49,664 / 16 = 3,104 exactly — good. Policy: snap soft anchors to block boundaries; hard anchors (turn ends) fall where they fall, and the residual partial block (<16 tokens) is recomputed — negligible.

**Respawn algorithm (exact steps):**
1. Acquire lease, epoch++ (CAS on ref `refs/lease/<seat>` or a lock file; git CAS via ref compare-and-swap push).
2. Resolve `refs/bus/<topic>/<seat>` → commit C → tree T, manifest M.
3. Verify: recompute T's hash from blobs (cheap: hashes already in objects; verification is inherent to git fetch). Check M.model.rev == local serving target; else full re-prefill path.
4. Build chain keys K_i = H(h_1..h_i) (streaming SHA-256 over concatenated hashes — cheap, no tokenization).
5. Call gateway `resume(chain=K_1..K_n, tail_tokens=draft_tail?)`. Gateway reports `hit_upto` block index.
6. Prefill tokens from hit point to head (usually zero or one partial block).
7. Optionally replay last draft tail as constrained prefix (accept draft tokens as forced prompt to save regeneration) — treaty flag `trust_drafts: bool` per seat class. Default false for reasoning seats, true for transcription-style seats.
8. Continue decode. Commit cadence: every assistant turn = canonical commit; every 128 generated tokens = draft blob push (async, best-effort).

**Cost ledger table (persists vs recomputes):**

| Item | Persisted? | Where | Recompute cost on respawn |
|---|---|---|---|
| Context segments | Yes | git blobs | 0 |

**Why "semantic" anchors matter vs fixed-interval:** fixed intervals (every 4k tokens) miss edit points; edits then invalidate to the previous interval boundary — average waste = half interval, worst = full interval, and worse: edits often want to touch specific turns (redact PII in turn 17), so turn-aligned anchors make the common cases exact-zero-waste. Sub-anchors cover the long-document case.

**Treaty clauses (write them as enforceable rules):**
T1 Immutability: once a blob is referenced by a committed tree, bytes never change. Enforcement: server-side hook rejects non-fast-forward + any tree whose parent shares a segment hash but differs in that blob's content (structurally impossible with git, but the hook also bans force-push on bus refs).
T2 Anchored edits: every splice commit must set FirstChangedAnchor to an existing anchor ordinal; hooks reject splices claiming anchor 0 when a deeper anchor matches (cost honesty).
T3 Key completeness: manifests without model.rev + tokenizer.hash are invalid; consumers must treat them as uncacheable.
T4 Atomic transitions: one commit per transition; seats never push intermediate trees.
T5 Lease exclusivity: single writer per seat ref per epoch; stale epochs rejected.
T6 Canonical bytes: CBOR-deterministic or canonical-JSON; violations fail hash verification downstream.
T7 Draft hygiene: drafts live outside the context tree; promotion to canonical requires a fresh commit by a live seat.
